paragraphs: Geologists call the impactor Theia, after the mythical mother of the moon goddess in Greek legend, though no trace of it survives as something separate from Earth. Apollo astronauts brought home lunar rock that is nearly identical, isotope for isotope, to Earth's own mantle, not the roughly even blend of two different bodies that simple impact models predict.

The newborn Moon also sat far closer to Earth than it does now, and a day on the young planet may have lasted only four to six hours. Tidal drag between the two bodies has pushed the Moon outward ever since, about 3.8 centimetres a year, and slowed Earth's spin as it goes; the 24 hour day is a comparatively recent arrangement.
